title: BPMN 2.0.2 documentation guidelines for process and collaboration generation
purpose: Operational paraphrases for an LLM that generates BPMN 2.0 XML from a process description.

normative_source.title: Business Process Model and Notation (BPMN), Version 2.0.2

profile_scope: Tasks, subprocesses, events, gateways and sequence flows
Common data objects and documentation artifacts
outside_prompt_scope: Vendor extensions and engine-specific deployment attributes
methodology_note: Concise paraphrases, not copied normative text. This common generation profile does not replace XSD validation or the full OMG specification.

rules.instruction: Return one complete, well-formed bpmn:definitions document and no surrounding explanation or Markdown fence.
Declare the BPMN model namespace http://www.omg.org/spec/BPMN/20100524/MODEL and a non-empty targetNamespace on bpmn:definitions.

Assign a unique XML id to every referenced element. Resolve all Ref attributes to existing, type-compatible elements. For example, a split gateway and the gateway that joins its branches get two different ids, such as Gateway_Approval_Split and Gateway_Approval_Join.
rules.pilot_note: example added in v2.2 after the pilot (2 duplicate gateway ids)

rules.instruction: Escape XML special characters in names, documentation and expressions. Do not emit undeclared prefixes, duplicate attributes or unclosed tags.
Do not add BPMN-DI, vendor extensions or execution-engine attributes unless the requested output explicitly requires them.

Follow the BPMN XML schema: never put a documentation element directly inside bpmn:definitions, and never nest a sequenceFlow inside a task, gateway or event. If you add an ioSpecification, it must contain its dataInput and dataOutput elements first, then at least one inputSet and one outputSet, even if empty: <bpmn:inputSet/><bpmn:outputSet/>.
Write default, sourceRef, targetRef, attachedToRef, processRef and messageRef as attributes, never as child elements, and give every association both a sourceRef and a targetRef.
Model every distinct activity, event, participant, decision, branch, loop, message and outcome stated in the description. Do not invent process facts.
Do not merge separately described actions into one task or split one stated action without a process reason. Preserve described dependencies.
Use short, faithful labels in the input language. Prefer verb-object activity names and meaningful business triggers or outcomes for events.
When the description does not justify a specialized construct, use the simplest compatible BPMN construct and do not guess missing semantics.
Represent each modeled internal workflow with bpmn:process. Use isExecutable=false unless execution-ready behavior is explicitly required and fully specified.
Keep each flow node and sequence flow inside its owning process or subprocess. Sequence flows never cross pool or subprocess boundaries.
Build a connected path from each modeled start to an end or intentionally continuing state. Avoid accidental disconnected flow nodes.
Allow multiple start or end events when the description has distinct triggers or outcomes. Do not force all outcomes into one end.

Give every process and every expanded subProcess its own explicit start event and end event. A trigger that occurs after the main flow (for example later feedback or a return) is joined to the main flow by a gateway, or modeled as an event subprocess or a separate process.
rules.source_clause: 10.2, 10.3.5; stricter than BPMN, which allows implicit start and end events in some cases

rules.instruction: Use bpmn:task for atomic work when the execution mode is unspecified. A task contains no internal flow.
Use bpmn:userTask for human work assisted by software and bpmn:manualTask for human work performed without an execution application.
Use bpmn:serviceTask for automated service work, bpmn:scriptTask for an explicit script, and bpmn:businessRuleTask for explicit rule evaluation.
Use bpmn:sendTask or bpmn:receiveTask when sending or waiting for a message is itself the modeled unit of work.
Distinguish message tasks from message events: a task models performed work; an event models a message occurrence affecting flow.
Model performer information only when responsibility is stated. Prefer lanes for ordinary organizational responsibility.
Several unconditional outgoing flows from one activity can all proceed. Use a gateway when the description requires a decision or synchronization.
Do not infer a task subtype only from a verb in its label; require supporting meaning in the full description.
Use bpmn:subProcess for a nested workflow belonging to its parent process; keep all internal nodes and flows inside it.
Use bpmn:callActivity only to invoke a separately defined reusable process or global task; make calledElement resolvable in the intended model context.
An ordinary embedded subprocess participates in normal sequence flow and may contain its own starts, ends, activities, gateways and flows.
For an event subprocess set triggeredByEvent=true, use exactly one triggered start event, and add no incoming or outgoing sequence flow.
Use standard loop or multi-instance characteristics only when repetition is explicit; choose sequential or parallel instances from the description.
Use transaction, ad-hoc or compensation behavior only when its specific semantics are explicitly described.
Inside an ordinary subProcess (embedded or called), use only a None start event; typed start triggers are reserved for top-level processes and event subprocesses.
Use start events for stated process triggers. A start event has no incoming sequence flow and is not the source of a message flow.
Use end events for terminal outcomes. An end event has no outgoing sequence flow and is not the target of a message flow.
Use an intermediate catch event when flow waits for a trigger and an intermediate throw event when flow emits or raises a result.
Use message events for directed participant communication, signal events for broadcasts, and timer events for stated dates, durations or cycles.
Use conditional, error, escalation, cancel, compensation, link, multiple or terminate events only when their specific semantics and placement are supported.
Use a none start when no trigger is stated. Never use a none start for an event subprocess.
Attach a boundary event with attachedToRef. Set cancelActivity=true when it interrupts the activity and false only for supported non-interrupting behavior.
Use an interrupting event-subprocess start when the parent scope stops; use non-interrupting only when the parent continues.
Use a terminate end only when all remaining activity in the current scope must end immediately.
Keep catch and throw direction consistent and avoid representing one occurrence redundantly as an equivalent adjacent task and event.
Attach to an activity boundary only these triggers: message, timer, escalation, conditional, signal, error, cancel, compensation or multiple. Never a none or link event.
An error boundary event is always interrupting (cancelActivity=true); a cancel boundary event is used only on a transaction subProcess.

Respect event positions: a none intermediate event is catch-only in normal flow and never on a boundary; link events are intermediate-only, thrown and caught in pairs at the same process level, and a catching link has no incoming sequence flow; terminate is an end event only.
For a message event, put messageRef on its bpmn:messageEventDefinition, never on the event element itself.
Use gateways to control divergence and convergence, never to represent work. Identify exclusive, inclusive, parallel, event-driven or complex behavior.
Use an exclusive split when exactly one data-based alternative runs. Add supported conditions and at most one default fallback.
Use an exclusive merge for alternative paths; it does not wait for inactive alternatives.
Use a parallel split when all outgoing branches start. Do not add decision conditions to parallel branches.
Use a parallel join when a shared continuation waits for all active parallel branches. Never use it to join mutually exclusive alternatives.
Use an inclusive split when one or more conditions can be true; use an inclusive join to synchronize only activated reachable branches.
Use an event-based gateway when the first occurring event selects the path. Target supported catching events or receive tasks, not ordinary tasks.
Use a complex gateway only for an explicitly described rule that XOR, OR and AND cannot express. Prefer separate split and join gateways for clarity.
Give the outgoing sequence flows of an event-based gateway no conditionExpression; the first occurring target event selects the path.
Every gateway either splits (two or more outgoing flows) or merges (two or more incoming flows); never give a gateway one incoming and one outgoing flow.
Use bpmn:sequenceFlow for execution order between flow nodes in the same process or subprocess scope; set valid sourceRef and targetRef values.
Only activities, gateways and events are sequence-flow endpoints. Never connect sequence flows to pools, lanes, data objects, groups or annotations.
Keep incoming and outgoing references consistent where used. Never add incoming flow to a start or outgoing flow from an end.
Use a boolean formal conditionExpression on a conditional flow only when the description supports the condition.
Reference a default flow with the source activity or gateway default attribute and give the default flow no conditionExpression.
Trace every split to continuations or endings. Add a join only when paths reunite and choose matching waiting semantics.
Represent loops only when repetition is stated and provide a meaningful exit unless endless behavior is explicit.
Create bpmn:collaboration when distinct participants interact and represent every participant as a bpmn:participant pool.
A white-box participant references its process with processRef. A black-box participant has no processRef and no modeled internal workflow.
Use sequence flows inside one participant process and message flows between different participants. Never use sequence flow across pools.
Direct each message flow from sender to receiver. Its endpoints must belong to different pools and be valid interaction nodes.
Do not attach message flows to lanes, gateways, data objects, groups or annotations; use participant boundaries or eligible flow nodes.
Create reusable bpmn:message elements and messageRef only when communication content or shared message identity matters.
Do not create separate pools for ordinary internal roles unless the description treats them as independent communicating participants.
Use lanes to partition one process by a stated role, department, system or responsibility; lanes are not separate processes.
Each lane flowNodeRef identifies a node in the owning process. Assign nodes according to stated responsibility and avoid arbitrary membership.
Sequence flows may cross lanes in one process. Use message flows across participant pools, never between lanes.
Lanes may be nested: a lane can contain a child laneSet that partitions it further; every flowNodeRef at any depth references nodes of the one owning process.
Put each flow node, including gateways and events, in exactly one lane.
Use dataObjectReference for process-instance data and dataStoreReference for persistent information available beyond one process instance.
Use data input and output associations between data and activities. Data associations do not define execution order.
Use text annotations and associations only for explanatory information; they do not control execution.
Use groups only for documentation or analysis categories; groups create no scope and change no flow behavior.
Verify XML syntax, namespaces, unique IDs, reference types, scopes, and all incoming and outgoing flow references.
Verify every start-to-end path, loop exit, branch condition and join; prevent deadlocks from incompatible branch and join semantics.
Verify processRef values, lane membership, message-flow endpoints and directions, and the prohibition on sequence flows between pools.
Compare the model with the description; remove unsupported elements and retain every explicitly stated alternative, outcome and collaboration.

When the description states a distinct action that occurs before a later recording or confirmation step: Model that action as its own activity in sequence before the later step; do not use an end event or another outcome element as its substitute.

When the description identifies actions or outcomes at distinct stages of a process: Label each BPMN element to reflect the action or outcome described at that stage; do not substitute a different action, a later-stage action, or an unsupported outcome.

When the description lists multiple actions in an order and does not indicate that they occur concurrently or independently: Model the actions in the stated order using sequence flows; do not use parallel branches unless the description supports concurrent or independent execution.

When the description says an activity may occur in addition to the main sequence: Model the activity on an optional path, using a decision gateway to determine whether it occurs, and rejoin the main sequence afterward.

When the description presents process activities in a stated order: Model the corresponding flow nodes in that order with sequence flows, connecting the start event to the initial activity and the final activity to the end event.

When the description presents activities whose execution order must be represented in BPMN: Represent that order with sequence flows that are direct children of the relevant process or subprocess scope; do not place sequence flows inside activities or other BPMN elements.

When the description explicitly states an activity’s action, object, recipient, or multiple coordinated actions: Preserve those stated details in the BPMN task label rather than omitting or substituting them.
When the description states that a participant selects or specifies inputs before a subsequent process action: Model that selection or specification as an explicit task before the dependent action.

When the description states that multiple follow-up activities after the same point must all occur, without describing them as alternatives: Model the activities as concurrent branches using a parallel gateway, and synchronize them with a parallel gateway before any subsequent activity that depends on all branches being complete.

When the description lists mutually exclusive ways to achieve an outcome: Model each stated alternative as a distinct activity on an exclusive-gateway branch, rather than combining the alternatives into one generic activity.

When the description says a participant performs a concrete action that initiates the process, rather than merely identifying an event that triggers it: Model the initiating action as a task after the start event and before the subsequent activity; do not represent the action only as a start event.

When the description specifies multiple distinct criteria or dimensions to be evaluated for an item.: Model each distinct evaluation as a separate activity rather than combining them into one activity.

When the description names multiple distinct activities together in one sentence or clause, including as a coordinated list: Represent each distinct activity as its own BPMN task, and preserve only the ordering or dependencies that the description states.

When the description states an activity or outcome whose surrounding context is already clear from the process flow: Use a concise BPMN label that preserves the activity or outcome, without adding explanatory context that does not distinguish it from other elements.

When the description states that review results can lead to feedback and a need to repeat an earlier review before proceeding.: Model providing feedback as an explicit activity, then use a decision gateway to route the repeat-review path back to the relevant review and the continuation path onward.

When the description identifies a decision, conditional action, or stopping outcome between activities: Model every stated transition with sequence flows, including flows into and out of gateways, and connect each outcome to its next step or end.

When the description says that a participant performs work by sending information to another participant: Model the sending as a task (use a send task when sending is itself the unit of work). Represent communication separately where appropriate; do not attach a message event definition to a task.

When the description distinguishes a participant’s instruction or assignment from the work that another participant is asked to perform: Label the BPMN activity as the instruction or assignment, preserving who directs whom; do not label it as though the directing participant were ordering or performing the requested work.

When the description states that a distinct activity is performed while other activities are in progress and that a later activity depends on their completion: Model the distinct activity and the other required work on concurrent branches, then synchronize those branches before the dependent activity.

When the description states that one activity is required while an independent activity is performed only when a condition holds: Model the activities as branches of an inclusive gateway, with the required activity on an always-taken branch and the optional activity on a conditional branch; use an inclusive join before any subsequent activity that depends on their completion.

When the description assigns activities to multiple roles or departments within one organization: Represent those responsibilities as lanes within one process, and place each stated activity in the lane of the role or department assigned to it; do not model those internal roles as separate participant pools or connect them with message flows.

When the description says that an interaction involves a set of external organizations but does not identify any organization individually: Represent the external participants at the level of identity the description supports; do not invent a specific numbered participant when the organizations are described only as a group.

When the description distinguishes activities or outcomes by their action, object, recipient, or stage: Use BPMN labels that preserve those stated distinctions rather than substituting a different action or outcome.

When the description describes communication or a signal between participants, while the underlying work or the receipt of that communication is already represented by activities or events: model the communication with a message flow between the appropriate existing sender and receiver nodes; do not add separate send or receive tasks solely to represent the exchange, or create message flows for physical movement that is not described as communication

When the description states an ongoing obligation and separately states that a later outcome can end or alter it: Model the obligation as recurring from the point it applies, and model the later outcome as changing or stopping future repetitions rather than gating whether the obligation is performed at all.

When the description specifies a quantity, frequency, or other scope constraint for an activity: Preserve that constraint in the BPMN activity label rather than weakening it to a more general activity.

When the description identifies multiple distinct items that must be prepared or verified before a later step.: Model each actionable preparation or verification as a separate activity before the dependent activity, preserving stated dependencies.
When the description describes a process to be represented in BPMN: Use XML-ID-valid values for BPMN element IDs, and ensure those IDs are unique within the document.

When the description says that a sequence of work must happen before the process proceeds to other described work: Model that sequence as connected to the main process flow, with its completion leading to the subsequent work, rather than as a detached start-to-end chain.

When the description says to order or otherwise obtain a specified item because that same item is unavailable: Model obtaining the specified item; do not substitute a related or alternative item unless the description supports that substitution.
When the description states a process trigger that precedes the first activity: Label the start event with the stated trigger, not with the activity that follows it.
When the description states the meaning of an activity, event, or gateway: label that BPMN element to preserve its stated meaning rather than substituting a generic or inferred alternative

When the description says that a returned result is refined repeatedly and the changes are sent back to the activity that produced it: Model a connected repetition loop: flow from receiving the result through assessment and refinement to sending the changes back to the producing activity, with the next returned result entering that cycle.

When the description identifies multiple distinct items as handled together in one stated action: Model each explicitly distinct item as its own activity, and use a parallel gateway to synchronize those activities before later work only when the description establishes that they occur together or are all required.

When the description states that an activity recurs at a fixed time interval: Model the elapsed interval with a timer intermediate catch event in the flow, and connect it to the recurring activity as required by the described repetition.
When the description makes a decision depend on comparing a value derived from other information: Model the necessary calculation or determination as an activity before the decision gateway.

When the description states that a participant performs an action that initiates the process: Model the described action as a task in the process flow; do not also represent that same action as a start event.

When the description says that the normal sequence and one or more retry paths after failed checks lead to the same earlier activity: Model the incoming alternatives through an exclusive merge gateway before that activity, rather than connecting each path directly to it.

renamed_from: bpmn_baseline (v1); renamed to reflect the normative source: the OMG BPMN 2.0.2 documentation
update_note: v2.2 (pilot round 2, Luna first models with v2.1: L3 failures 7 -> 3, L1 failures 4 -> 5): XML-06 gives the exact inputSet/outputSet snippet, XML-07 adds messageRef to the attribute list, and the existing rule XML-03 gets one example (distinct ids for a split and its join). No rule added. v2.1 states six rules explicitly after a pilot run: the validator's errors in 165 first models (GPT-6 Luna, Claude Haiku 5.5, GPT-6.1 Sol, documentation guidelines only) showed which rules of the specification and of its XML schema the generator broke. Only validator results were used, never a reference model. Each new rule carries its source_clause and pilot_evidence (number of failures it addresses). v2.0 note: v2.0 adds five rules identified by a systematic gap check of the catalogue against the full OMG PDF (formal/13-12-09): SUB-07, GW-09, EVT-11, EVT-12, EVT-13, LANE-04. Each carries its source clause. Cleanup: each v2.1 rule keeps only what the 76 earlier rules did not state; errors already covered by an earlier rule (unique ids XML-03, existing references FLOW-01/XML-03, parallel join of exclusive branches GW-05, lane of the owning process LANE-02, connected paths PROC-03) are not repeated. XML-06 corrected to match the schema exactly (no documentation in definitions; ioSpecification needs inputSet and outputSet).
